questions.q: Answer in one word or phrase: (i) How is India described in terms of religion? (ii) What does the Constitution of India forbid regarding religion?
questions.answer: (i) Secular, multi-religious (and multicultural). (ii) Any discrimination on grounds of religion.

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: (i) Hygiene is the practice of keeping oneself and the ________ clean to prevent illness. (ii) Age-wise dietary guidelines for nutrients are known as the Recommended Dietary ________.
State True or False: (i) Legally, children are those under 18 years of age. (ii) The Maternity Benefit Amendment Act, 2017 makes childcare facilities at workplaces optional.
questions.answer: (i) True. (ii) False — it makes them mandatory.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: What is meant by religious plurality? How does it affect children?
questions.answer: Religious plurality means many religions — Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism, Jainism, Islam, Christianity and tribal religions — coexist in secular India. Religion shapes children's dress, food, customs and festivals and their sense of identity, so schools should know these practices and connect home festivities with school.

questions.q: How does the socio-economic status of a family affect a child's development?
questions.answer: It decides the family's means and access to resources. Well-off families can afford better schools and materials; poverty often comes with illiteracy, poor childcare and less constructive beliefs. Children in long-term poverty show poor attention span, poor retention and more developmental delays.

questions.q: Explain the influence of maternal health on the health of a child.
questions.answer: Healthy children are born to healthy mothers, and infants depend on breast milk for the first six months. At least 20% of the disease burden of under-fives is linked to maternal health and nutrition and care at delivery; a baby whose mother dies at birth is less likely to survive.

questions.q: Differentiate between stunting and wasting.
questions.answer: Both are signs of under-nutrition. Stunting is low height for age, showing long-term malnutrition and lack of stimulation; wasting is low weight for height, showing recent or acute lack of food. NFHS-4 found 38.4% of under-fives stunted.

questions.q: What are child-rearing practices?
questions.answer: Practices grounded in cultural patterns and beliefs that parents and caregivers adopt for the care and upbringing of a child — for example, birth customs, confinement of the mother, feeding and weaning ceremonies. They depend on the child's age and the health and nutritional risks the child faces.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: What is the impact of early childhood on subsequent life?
questions.answer: Early childhood is a sensitive period shaped by nature and nurture, when the brain grows fastest; children 'use it or lose it' and benefit from 'serve and return' interaction. A stimulating, caring, healthy environment gives lasting gains. Adversity — poverty, neglect, abuse, frequent illness — leads to social, emotional, behavioural and school-adjustment problems, even mental-health problems or delinquency, and such adults may repeat poor parenting. Sensitive parenting, family and community support and good childcare can moderate these effects.

or.q: What is the constitutional view of childhood in India?
or.answer: The Constitution treats children's survival, development and protection as rights and duties: Article 14 equality before law; 15 no discrimination and special provisions for children; 21A free and compulsory education for 6–14; 24 no child below 14 in factories, mines or hazardous work; 39 children not abused or forced into unsuitable work and given chances to develop in freedom and dignity; 45 free and compulsory education; 46 interests of weaker sections; 47 nutrition and public health; 51A(k) parents' duty to educate their children.

questions.q: How does maternal mortality affect child survival and development?
questions.answer: Maternal mortality is the death of a woman from complications of pregnancy and childbirth (or within 42 days). A baby whose mother dies at birth is less likely to survive, and children who lose their mothers are ten times more likely to die within two years. It depends on the mother's age, health and wellbeing; early marriage (before 18) makes robust motherhood less likely and raises IMR.

or.q: Why is breastfeeding considered important for the health of both mother and child?
or.answer: Breast milk is a complete, wholesome food for the newborn for the first six months and protects against infection, lowering illness and deaths; it also gives touch, comfort and bonding. NFHS-4 notes early breastfeeding within an hour of delivery. For the mother it builds the bond with the baby, and communities have customs and foods to support lactation.

questions.q: How do families need to accommodate children with special conditions, and what challenges do they face?
questions.answer: Children with disabilities are among the most excluded; many do not complete primary education. Families must meet their special requirements, which often need extra care, time, money and therapy from parents, and help them join mainstream schools. Siblings and other children need counselling to understand differences and reach out with empathy.

or.q: What are the challenges faced by migrant children, particularly those of families employed in the unorganised sector?
or.answer: An estimated 4–6 million children are affected by migration. Their families face exclusion from basic services, exploitative work (no minimum wages, no social security), gender-based wage discrimination and denial of maternity rights and childcare. Seasonal migration disrupts schooling and often denies the child's right to education.

questions.q: How does India's multi-cultural society contribute to diverse social environments for children?
questions.answer: India is a pluralistic society where people of different religions, languages, castes, tribes and economic backgrounds live together, across varied regions (Himalayas, plains, deserts, coasts). These differences in beliefs, resources, food, dress and customs give children very different experiences of childhood; some groups are disadvantaged by caste discrimination, poverty or remoteness.

or.q: What factors contribute to the poor health and living conditions of children in India?
or.answer: Uneven distribution of economic resources, lack of access and awareness lead to ill health, high-density living and unhygienic conditions. Other causes are malnutrition (stunting, wasting), infection and lack of sanitation and clean water, poor maternal health and early marriage, and gender bias against girls in health care and nutrition.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: Briefly explain the factors affecting childhood.
questions.answer: Heredity: genes from parents decide height, body structure, eye colour, hair texture, partly intelligence and aptitudes, and some diseases. Environment: physical and psychological stimulation, positive modelling and loving relationships build skills and aspiration. Exercise: play builds muscle strength and bone mass and helps children reach milestones. Sex of the child: boys and girls grow at different rates, especially near puberty. Nutrition: a balanced diet is needed for growth and repair; protein deficiency causes stunting, overeating obesity. Familial influence: consistent, responsive adults build attachment; stress, neglect or too much control harm development. Geographical influences: neighbourhood parks, libraries and peers shape interests. Socio-economic status: poverty limits access and long-term poverty causes more delays. Adequate rest and sleep also matter.
questions.note: April 2023 asked: explain hereditary and environmental factors and their interrelationship.

questions.q: Describe the factors influencing children's health.
questions.answer: Hygiene: personal (washing hands after the toilet, brushing teeth, bathing, clean clothes, cut nails, covering mouth and nose) and environmental (no stagnant water, covered drinking water). Sanitation: safe treatment and disposal of excreta and sewage to stop faecal-oral spread of disease. Nutrition: a balanced diet of proteins, carbohydrates, fats, minerals, vitamins, fibre and water as per the RDA; malnutrition shows as stunting, wasting, underweight, micronutrient deficiency or obesity. Immunisation: vaccines (BCG, OPV, DPT, measles, MMR, etc.) on a fixed schedule protect from infections, as with the elimination of polio. Maternal health: healthy mothers have healthy babies; good nutrition in pregnancy and two years after birth gives children the best chance to survive.
